title: Chemistry, not medicine, defeated America's patent medicine epidemic
dek: Nineteenth-century American patent medicines grew through anti-establishment sentiment and newspaper advertising; the real exposé came not from advances in germ theory but from analytical chemistry finally revealing what was actually in the bottle.
why: This traces 'snake oil salesman' back to its real history and shows how today's supplements, biohacking, and influencer marketing follow the same playbook.
who: Anyone interested in the history of consumer protection, the evolution of medical regulation, or understanding how today's supplement and biohacking marketing operates.
skip: The opening section featuring Clark Stanley's autobiography can be skipped without losing the thread of the argument.

points.h: Regulators caught snake oil and fined it twenty dollars
points.body: In 1917, federal chemists finally analyzed Clark Stanley's "snake oil" and found no actual snake—just mineral oil, beef tallow, capsaicin, camphor, and turpentine. His fine was $20 (roughly $523 today). For a decades-long con complete with live-snake demonstrations at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, the penalty barely qualified as a wrist-slap.

points.h: Anti-elite backlash stripped medical licenses from nearly all American doctors
points.body: Between 1820 and 1840, most American states abolished medical licensing. By 1845, only three states still required it. The pressures converged: Eastern medical schools couldn't produce enough rural physicians; the era's "heroic medicine" relied on massive bloodletting and forced vomiting (Benjamin Rush advocated draining roughly 80% of a patient's blood), so its authority was already questionable; and Jacksonian democracy held that professional licensure was inherently undemocratic—ordinary people should choose their own treatments.

points.h: Newspapers stayed afloat by running patent medicine advertisements
points.body: Nineteenth-century newspapers depended on patent medicine ads to survive. It was mutually beneficial: papers sold space, medicine makers reached a national audience. During the Civil War, the same product would run separate ads aimed at Union and Confederate readers, and marketers invented early clickbait—headlines like "South Carolina in Upheaval—General Beauregard Captured" that led readers to cough syrup advertisements.

points.h: Snake oil's formula was likely stolen from Chinese immigrants
points.body: Clark Stanley claimed he learned snake oil from Hopi Indians, but the episode suggests he probably copied it from nineteenth-century Chinese immigrants who brought their own snake-oil remedy to America—made from Chinese water snakes and applied topically for joint pain. Later research confirmed these oils actually contained omega-3s with genuine anti-inflammatory effects. Indigenous remedies were routinely stolen by white entrepreneurs, who then repackaged them with invented tales of tribal wisdom.

points.h: Fraudsters learned to speak the language of germ theory
points.body: After the popular health movement faded, science regained public trust—but fraudsters didn't lose; they learned the lexicon. When germ theory emerged, so did products billed as "disinfectants" and "microbe killers," often advertised as "Pasteur's favorite." Contrary to what you might expect, patent medicine sales didn't drop as microbiology advanced; they continued climbing. Scientific progress didn't stop the fake medicine market—it just gave con artists better vocabulary.

points.h: Patients believed the most bitter medicines worked the hardest
points.body: Many patent medicines deliberately included bitter compounds like quinine because widespread belief held that potency correlated with poor taste. Others created dependency through alcohol, cocaine, or opium. Some contained dangerous ingredients like belladonna, mercury, or arsenic. Placebo effects are genuine physiological phenomena, not mere psychology—which helps explain why customers remained loyal to useless medicines, convinced of their own healing.

points.h: Analytical chemistry exposed fakes in ways that laws never could
points.body: The real breakthrough wasn't medical knowledge or legislation—it was analytical chemistry, the first tool capable of opening a bottle and revealing its actual contents. When Radom's Microbe Killer was analyzed, it tested at 99.381% water with just a touch of red wine for coloring. Yet the 1906 Pure Food and Drug Act was weak: it only required manufacturers to list alcohol, opium, and similar ingredients by quantity. In the year the act passed, over 50,000 patent medicine brands were sold—up from 28,000 in 1905.

points.h: The supplement industry is heading toward five hundred billion dollars
points.body: The American patent medicine industry was valued at $74.5 million in 1904—approximately $228 billion in today's purchasing power, and projected to approach $500 billion by 2033. The episode argues this isn't primarily a legal problem but a permanent aspect of human nature: people always crave an inexpensive, simple, painless, fast-acting universal cure. That appetite hasn't diminished in the era of supplements, biohacking, and influencer commerce.
